title: Sliding Window
overview:
Sliding Window is a problem-solving technique used to process a continuous range of elements in an array or string.

Instead of repeatedly calculating or checking the same elements, we maintain a window over a portion of the data and move it as needed.

For example:

Array:   [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6]
          └─────────┘
           Window 1

Array:   [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6]
              └─────────┘
               Window 2

Array:   [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6]
                  └─────────┘
                   Window 3

For a window size of 3:

Window 1 → [1] [2] [3]
Window 2 →     [2] [3] [4]
Window 3 →         [3] [4] [5]
Window 4 →             [4] [5] [6]

The window represents a continuous part of the array or string.
whyUse:
Many problems ask us to find something about continuous elements, such as:

Maximum sum of a subarray of size k
Minimum or maximum value within a range
Longest substring satisfying a condition

A straightforward solution may repeatedly process the same elements.

Sliding Window avoids much of this repeated work by adding elements when the window expands and removing elements when it moves forward.
howItWorks: There are two common types of sliding windows.

Fixed-Size Window

The window always contains the same number of elements.

For example, for a window size of 3:

Array:   [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
          └─────────┘
           Window

When the window moves one position:

Array:   [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
              └─────────┘
               Window

One element leaves the window and one new element enters.

This is useful for problems such as finding the maximum sum of k consecutive elements.

Variable-Size Window

The size of the window can grow or shrink depending on a condition.

For example:

Array:   [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
          ↑           ↑
        left        right

The right pointer expands the window.

If the current window no longer satisfies the required condition, left moves forward to shrink it.

This is commonly used for problems involving longest or shortest valid subarrays or substrings.

patterns.title: Common Sliding Window Pattern
patterns.description:
A typical sliding window uses two boundaries:

left  → beginning of the window
right → end of the window

The general idea is:

Expand window
      ↓
Check condition
      ↓
Condition satisfied?
   ↙          ↘
 Yes           No
  ↓             ↓
Update answer   Shrink window
                ↓
             Continue

For example, when looking for the longest valid substring:

String:  A  B  C  D  E
         ↑        ↑
       left      right

We expand right while the window remains valid.

When the condition becomes invalid, we move left forward until the window becomes valid again.

notes: Sliding Window can often reduce a solution from O(n²) to O(n) because each element is usually added to and removed from the window only a limited number of times.
The exact space complexity depends on whether additional data structures, such as a hash map or frequency array, are needed to maintain information about the current window.

keyTakeaways: Sliding Window processes a continuous range of elements in an array or string.
A window can be fixed-size or variable-size.
The window moves by adjusting its boundaries, usually using left and right.
It avoids repeatedly processing the same elements.
It is commonly used for subarray and substring problems.
Sliding Window can often reduce a brute-force O(n²) solution to O(n).
